name: Ura (Papua New Guinea)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Baining-family Ura; only subclassification notes (Hausdorf 2022) surfaced, no grammar located

new_statements.quote: Stress is not contrastive in Ura; rather it appears to be basically penultimate but affected by syllable weight. Primary stress must be on one of the last two syllables. It will be on the first heavy one; or if neither is heavy, on the penultimate syllable. A heavy syllable in Ura is one with a heavy rhyme, either containing a branching nucleus or a coda. [...] We observe secondary stress emerging in quadrisyllabic words, on the initial syllable. [...] A rough estimate would be that twenty percent of Ura words have irregular stress (if indeed the regular pattern has been correctly identified in this section).
new_statements.citation: Stanton, Lee. 2007. Topics in Ura phonology and morphophonology, with lexicographic application. MA thesis, University of Canterbury.
new_statements.locator: §4.5 'Stress', thesis p. 4—82 (PDF p. 94); secondary stress §4.5.3 p. 4—84; exceptions §4.5.4 pp. 4—84/85; loanwords §4.5.6 p. 4—86; orthographic summary §6.1 p. 6—117

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress in a two-syllable window at the right edge: primary stress falls on the final syllable if it is heavy (long vowel/diphthong or coda), otherwise on the penult (penult heaviness is irrelevant except as the default; a heavy antepenult does not attract stress, ex. 301). Default penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress reported on the initial syllable of quadrisyllabic (polymorphemic) words (§4.5.3, exx. 306–309); hard to determine in some items.
new_statements.exceptions: Roughly twenty percent of words estimated irregular (§4.5.4, Table 8 in appendix); epenthetic [a] between stem and suffix sometimes ignored for stress, especially in /ŋ/-final stems (§4.5.5); loanwords from English/Tok Pisin are mostly penultimate despite heavy final syllables (§4.5.6); author states the pattern 'should be taken as tentative rather than decisive' and that stress was difficult to gauge consistently across speakers.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (mono- and polymorphemic words elicited in citation/wordlist form; ~600-item wordlist and texts); no phrase-level statement. Tone stated not contrastive (§4.1 p. 4—20). Data mainly from speakers in the Gaulim area, Gazelle Peninsula.
new_statements.identity_note: Stanton 2007 describes Ura (Uramät) of the Gaulim area, Gazelle Peninsula, East New Britain — the same language as Glottolog urap1240 / ISO uro; the author notes only minor phonetic variation between areas and generations and no named dialects. Not to be confused with urap1239 (Urapmin, Ok family) which the earlier scan handled separately.

sources.note: §4.5 (pp. 4—81 to 4—86): stress not contrastive; primary stress on the first heavy syllable among the last two, otherwise penultimate (heavy = branching nucleus or coda); secondary stress on the initial syllable of quadrisyllables; ~20% of words exceptional; loanwords mostly penultimate even with heavy final; pattern described as tentative. Also §6.1 p. 6—117 (orthographic summary) and §4.1 p. 4—20: 'Tone is not contrastive in Ura.' fetched sources from the Wayback Machine capture (2015-01-18) of the open UC Research Repository handle 10092/940, which is Cloudflare-blocked from our machine.
